article.title: French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
article.full_text: France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election. Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy. “The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said. The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said. “They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.” Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. “The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.” He listed several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to influence perceptions of the Israel-Gaza war, to accusations that Azerbaijan stirred up tensions amid deadly riots in the French Pacific territory New Caledonia. Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest man and owner of the social media platform X. “There are massive online harassment campaigns launched by Elon Musk against European leaders in order to influence debates by exploiting the virality of his social media platform.” Musk did not reply to a request for comment. Barrot also cited the protests that have rocked France in recent weeks, as schoolchildren, students and trade unionists blockaded schools and marched through cities. The events, said Barrot, had been exploited by “hostile narratives” from Russia, China and Iran, as well as those associated with the Maga movement in the US. Last week Musk and the US president, Donald Trump, weighed in on the protests in France, seeking to recast them through a lens of mass migration and brushing aside protesters’ demands for better school conditions. Barrot said his government was working to respond to a reality in which paid or commissioned influencers sought to explore the viral reach of digital platforms. “The Kremlin’s goal is explicitly stated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favour of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging on this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad’ based on whether they align with their own interests,” he said. The French minister’s remarks come days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was “clear” that Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum. Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign entities. “We are uncompromising, because it is clear to us that they undermine the nation’s fundamental interests,” he said. “We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty.”

article.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
article.full_text: Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday. The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist. Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week. But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”. “The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study. “Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said. He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV). The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints. “When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”. She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.” Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”. Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark. In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study. “It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University. It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.” When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.

article.title: The IMF says we need to make ‘urgent choices’. But are they choices the Albanese government is willing to make?
article.full_text: The IMF on Tuesday released its latest World Economic Outlook, suggesting “Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices”. But the choices are ones a government wishing to win an election would likely ignore. The IMF, as a rule, always sees a need to cut spending and lower taxes. Given its history of lending money to countries in severe debt, that’s no shock, and, even if the austerity it prescribed ruined lives, the IMF is very much in the Margaret Thatcher “the medicine is harsh but the patient requires it” mould. That’s important given what it thinks are “urgent choices”. But first we always get a sense of how the IMF see the world when we look at the titles of its outlook. A year ago, it was Global Economy in Flux, Prospects Remain Dim, followed by Global Economy: Steady amid Divergent Forces. That, as I suggested at the time, was an extraordinary way to describe a world where Donald Trump was threatening Greenland and had just launched an insurgency into Venezuela. Since then, of course, there has been nothing “steady”, and the IMF outlooks went from Global Economy in the Shadow of War to Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology. Now apparently all is resilient despite the strain. For Australia the update slightly downgrades forecasts for economic growth over the next couple years. The big downgrades, though, came last October, before the US and Israel’s war on Iran: Click here if this graph does not display The downgrades since April are all margin of error stuff. The forecast for economic growth this year has Australia in the top half of the advanced nations of the OECD, and only behind the US among the G7 nations: Click here if this graph does not display Similarly, the forecast for inflation is not much changed from April – up a bit, but the IMF still thinks inflation will be below 3% by next year: Click here if this graph does not display There has been a report that this will mean Australia’s inflation is among the highest across the OECD next year. But, to be honest, so long at it is between 2% and 3%, arguing over who has the lowest is pretty silly. And yes, Australia is expected to see its unemployment rise by more than most OECD economies but it will remain lower here than three of the G7. Click here if this graph does not display I also would happily take the IMF’s prediction for unemployment in 2026 of 4.4% and 4.7% next year, given currently (at least until Thursday) it is 4.6%. Over the next five years (at which point predictions get very ropey) the IMF sees pretty weak growth, inflation within the target range and unemployment not going above 4.8% Click here if this graph does not display Would that be so bad? I’d prefer unemployment closer to 4% but, right now, given the ructions in the economy, steady inflation below 3% and unemployment lower than 4.8% is a pretty nice combination. These things never come true though (see above), so perhaps more relevant are the “urgent choices” that the IMF thinks needs to be made. One chapter of the outlook examines how governments respond to cost of living shocks such as the US-Israel war on Iran or Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It notes government can either provide income support to (mostly) low-income households or it can suppress prices by, for example, cutting the fuel excise or subsidising energy costs (two policies the Albanese government undertook). The IMF found that (and prepare to be shocked) price-suppressing policies suppressed prices and thus lowered current inflation and also the inflationary expectations of the following year. By contrast, providing households with income support raised consumption by more (again not a shock) but it actually raised inflation not only in the current year but the expectation for inflation in the following year: Click here if this graph does not display Now you might think that makes it obvious that if you want to lower the burden of inflation the best policy is to suppress prices and actually lower inflation.
